The Ismail Family Shooting: Mistaken Identity

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
This is about what happens when those we trust to protect us may have instead caused irreparable harm.

Unique Selling Point:
OPENING SCENE
Two juxtapositioned Visuals:
A white VW Polo glides down a suburban road. Inside, the mother reaches over to hold her child’s hand. The father, driving, glances back with a smile. Passing the graveyard.
VO: Moments before their lives would change forever, a husband, his pregnant wife, and their toddler were quietly talking about death. Just a week earlier, a relative had been laid to rest in the cemetery they were now passing. None of them knew that, seconds later, they too would be knocking on death’s door.
CUT TO: NIU police officers gearing up — hands loading magazines, a rifle’s bolt clacking into place. Police radio: “We’re looking for a silver Etios.”
The screech of brakes.
A deafening volley of gunshots.
Screams pierce the chaos.
Photos from scene after shooting… emergency lights and noises…
(Presenter VO):— The years that followed that moment have been riddled with questions…
SOUNDUPS: QUESTIONS
Two versions of that night emerged — one from the shooters, one from the family in the line of fire.
Who is telling the truth?
(Presenter LINK): This is about what happens when those we trust to protect us may have instead caused irreparable harm. But it’s more than that — it’s about justice delayed, and perhaps denied. Five years on from the shooting that tore the Ismail family’s lives apart, no one has been held to account. And the reasons may be as disturbing as the shooting itself.
FADE TO BLACK…
ACT 1: The basic story
(Presenter VO): A cold winter Thursday evening — around 7 p.m., July 16, 2020 — settles over Berea, Durban.
Omar Ismail drives home with his wife, Asma, and their toddler, Yusraa, after visiting Asma’s mother.
Ten weeks pregnant with their second child — a little boy they plan to name Essa — Asma sits in the back seat beside Yusraa, strapped into her car seat.
(Asma):
(Omar):
(Presenter VO): A few hundred metres from their home on Sheringham Road, a white unmarked BMW suddenly swerves into the road. A man jumps out, gun in hand.
(Asma):
(Omar):
(Presenter VO): Omar ducks beneath the steering wheel to avoid the bullets, unable to see clearly — their silver Polo hits the BMW and they drift into a streetlamp.
(Asma):
(Omar):
(Presenter VO): Then… silence. Yusraa is screaming. While trying to make sense of what just happened. Omar lifts his head — another shot rings out from behind. The bullet tears through the headrest, hitting him in the back of the head. He slumps forward. Asma, her right leg hanging by a thread clings to consciousness. She calls her mother, Rehana.
Visual: Mother answering the phone, horrified.
Rehana: It was close to their house — maybe five minutes away. I drove straight there.
(Presenter VO): What she finds is an unexpected twist.
Rehana: “When I arrived, the men told me they were police officers.
(Presenter VO): But that's not the only strange information she learns.
Rehana: But there was something wrong — no ambulance, no flashing lights. They hadn’t called emergency services. It had been nearly ten minutes, and I was the first to phone for an ambulance.”
Visual: Photos of vehicles and bullet damage at the scene.
(Presenter VO): Asma’s heart stops at St Augustine’s Hospital, but she’s resuscitated.
Yusraa - shot in her arm - was luckily saved by her car seat.
Omar was shot four times, including his head, and was left temporarily blind.
Visual: Timelapse sky, fading to black.
(Presenter LINK) with family: “Months later, Omar was left with shrapnel in his brain, and risks paralysis if surgeons attempt removal. Asma lost her right leg and she still has shrapnel in her left.
(Presenter VO): Asma works as a lab technician, and standing for hours is painful. Omar, a bookkeeper, has struggled to find employment since the shooting, his current job is made more difficult by his partial blindness and severe headaches.
(Presenter LINK) at Intersection: But what really happened at this T-junction of Hill and Sheringham Roads? The story the police would later tell would make the family question everything. This is their story according to their pleas and affidavits.
Fade to black…
ACT 2: The Two Versions
Military-style, authoritative tone; overlay of visuals and VO
ON SCREEN: 16 July 2020…
Presenter VO (dramatic tone): “Six police officers are on the hunt for a group of hijackers. On-Screen Visuals: Fade into uniformed officers preparing for deployment.
(Presenter VO): They’re members of the National Intervention Unit (NIU)—an elite, intelligence-driven tactical unit in the South African Police Service trained for high-risk operations such as armed crime, and violent syndicate activity. They report directly to the National Commissioner of Police.
(Presenter VO): Crime Intelligence’s information is that the syndicate’s suspects are in the Berea area—travelling in a silver or grey Toyota Etios sedan with cloned plates.
Visual overlay: Show a schematic of two unmarked vehicles in convoy.
(Presenter LINK): The Warrant officers wore uniforms but their two vehicles were unmarked. In the BMW (white 1 series) was Talent Mseleku the driver, Yogandran Munsami and Donovan Naidoo. Following them in a VW Kombi (silver) was driver Menzi Michael Shabalala and Mathew Nathoo.
ON SCREEN graphic: Display 18:45 over a map.
(Presenter VO): As the convoy drove South along Hill Street toward Sheringham Road, the officers in the BMW noticed a silver VW Polo - that’s the Ismail family - but ALSO the silver Toyota Etios they’ve been looking for behind it. It’s implied the Polo and Etios were stationary when the police came across them. They say —”the hijackers alighted their vehicle and were about to hijack the VW Polo when NIU members intervened.” [page 2, iii].
Presenter LINK (raising questions): “The police’s descriptions of the hijackers is scant. They’re male, although the number remains unknown. All that’s reported is that they were wearing balaclavas and were moving in a crouched-over manner toward the VW Polo’s rear. [no where does it say they were stationary]
(Presenter VO): Munsami leapt from the front passenger seat of the BMW, shouting ‘POLICE!’ They say the hijackers then opened fire — and that’s when the gunfight began.
The police say their shots were aimed at the hijackers in the Toyota Etios, and that the Ismail family’s Polo was caught in the crossfire. They say it wasn’t their bullets that struck Omar, Asma, and Yusraa — but the hijackers. And even if their own rounds did cause the injuries, their defense is that it was a lawful shooting, undertaken to protect the family from a ‘dangerous situation.’
(Presenter LINK): The officers frame their actions as those of ‘peace officers’ defending themselves and the public. Their legal defence even leans on an obscure doctrine — volenti non fit injuria — which means Omar knowingly drove into the line of fire.
(Presenter VO): The hijackers fled down Sheringham Road. Shabalala, in the VW Kombi, returned fire while Naidoo shot the Etios’s rear tyre. Mseleku attempted to give chase, but due to the collision with the Polo the BMW was too damaged.
After they say they checked on the Polo’s occupants and called for medical assistance.
Presenter LINK to next section: Who’s really telling the truth? Carte Blanche has sifted through witness statements, ballistics tests, expert analyses, and hours of CCTV footage — uncovering evidence that punches glaring holes in the police’s account. And it starts with the shocking revelation: Was there a silver Etios?
TEXT ON SCREEN: Was there an Etios?
(Omar): No car was following us.
(Presenter VO):There are nine CCTV camera angles covering different points along this route.
They reveal the police’s timeline is out by 15 minutes, but when you track the Ismail family’s Polo across multiple points… even a few hundred metres before the shooting…the evidence is in what you don’t see. No Etios... In fact, there’s no footage of an Etios in any footage.
EXPERT INTRO
(EXPERT): CCTV footage doesn’t lie — timestamps are locked, and the sequence can be independently verified. This raises serious questions about the police version.
(Presenter VO): But it does show something the police left out — the VW Kombi missed the turn into Hill Street, and therefore, was about a minute behind the BMW. That likely means they weren’t there when the first shots were fired — at least not as the police’s version infers.
VISUAL: TEXT ON SCREEN: What did witnesses see?
(Presenter VO): There were many witnesses like blah blah who we met at the scene.
It's what two witnesses for the Ismail family saw, or didn't see, is critical.
LINK: Witness One, watching from his balcony, says he saw the whole incident unfold. He describes only three vehicles: the Ismail family’s Polo, and the two police vehicles. No other cars. He also says the police were firing directly at the Polo. Could this have been a case of mistaken identity?
(Expert): This points to a likely case of mistaken identity. From the front, a silver VW Polo and a silver Toyota Etios can look similar — but if there was no Etios at all, it suggests the police account of suspects and their behaviour was fabricated.
Presenter LINK: Witness Two only heard the gunfire. When he dared to look outside, he also saw no Etios. But he noticed something else — something darker. The officers were collecting their spent cartridges. Was there a coverup?
(Expert): That’s scene tampering. Removing shell casings prevents ballistic experts from matching a bullet to a specific gun — and to the officer who fired it.
TEXT ON SCREEN: What do the bullets and scene say?
Another graphic - we also have photos from SAPS scene recreation report.
(Presenter VO): “There are two ballistic reports: the state’s and the family’s. Both agree there were no shell casings, but the eight R4/R5 rifle rounds they did find, were likely from police weapons. But the family’s expert found something more — a ninth bullet from a 9mm pistol. Remember that extra bullet for later.
LINK: Both experts also agree on this: there was no crossfire. All the shots came from the direction of the police. The family’s expert says the Polo was deliberately targeted; the state’s expert stops short of saying that outright — but the implication is clear.
(Presenter VO): A SAPS scene reconstruction aligns with the Ismail family’s version confirming the Polo was moving and not stationary as the police’s version implies. And that the direction of fire was at the Polo, this resulted in Omar likely panicking and losing control of the vehicle.
(Expert): That’s a critical point — it places the Ismail family directly in the line of police fire from the outset. It was because they shot at him that he ducked.
LINK: If this was a case of mistaken identity, when did the officers realise they had the wrong car — at the moment Omar’s Polo slammed into their BMW, or when they heard the baby screaming? The missing shell casings and a specific moment during the shooting cast a dark shadow over the officers’ actions.
Asma: That must have been when the officers realised something was wrong — what hijacker would have a baby in the car? My husband then popped up his head.
VO: Omar had been crouched low behind the steering wheel, then raised his head.
Omar: I just wanted to check on them.
Presenter: Can you remember that?
Omar: Yes.
Asma: I was already calling my mother, panicking, trying to get help. And then I saw one of the men with a gun coming closer to the window — and he fired into the driver’s headrest. Omar slumped forward.
Rehana (Asma’s mother): I thought my son-in-law was dead.
VO: Could this have been from the missing 9mm round?
Rehana kept having this question running through her mind.
Rehana: Why hadn’t the police called an ambulance?
Link: Was there a coverup? Missing shell casings, no ambulances called, the extra bullet round, when and how Omar was shot… It begs the logical question: If the Ismail family didn’t survive, would these events have died with them?
ACT 3:
TEXT ON SCREEN: What does the Law say?
(Expert): It’s also important to consider who fired first. If there were no hijackers, the first shots could only have come from the police. That’s a serious problem — it opens the door to attempted murder charges. Our law is clear: force can only be used in self-defence or to protect others. That clearly doesn’t apply here.
Presenter LINK: And yet, years later, the case has stalled.
Omar: The NPA says it is still waiting for the Hawks to act. IPID — the Independent Police Investigative Directorate — has also investigated, but that too has gone nowhere.
(Expert): When IPID arrives on a scene, their job is to secure the shooting site, investigate whether evidence — like shell casings — was tampered with, and confiscate the firearms used. If those steps weren’t followed immediately, it undermines the entire investigation.
Presenter VO: But what about the civil case? That case names the Police Ministry itself, that seeks to awards money to the family for the damage this has caused.
Omar: It was supposed to go ahead in September last year, then again this September. But they keep delaying it — getting new lawyers. Instead of settling with us, it’s costing the state hundreds of thousands. I don’t know if they’re hoping we’ll die or something before that from our injuries.
(Expert): In law, there’s a provision against wasteful and fruitless expenditure. The police should recognise they have no realistic chance of winning and settle with the family. Continuing to fight is already costing taxpayers hundreds of thousands.
(Presenter VO): We asked the police how much they’ve spent defending the civil case.
[N2](Presenter LINK): And we wanted to know why there have been such long delays in investigating these officers. Is it simply inefficiency, indifference, or bureaucracy? Or… could it be because two of the officers involved in the shooting are celebrated police heroes?
That’s why I’m standing here — on this stretch of Durban’s N2 highway near Nandi Drive.
TEXT ON SCREEN: August 4, 2017.
TEXT ON SCREEN: August 4, 2017
(Presenter VO): In August 2017, two of the officers now implicated in the Ismail family shooting — Donovan Naidoo and Yogandran Munsamy — were involved in a high-profile shootout. In that daylight battle, five armed suspects were intercepted; three “died at the scene,” while two survived and were arrested. Civilians and officers were injured in the chaos. Naidoo and Munsamy were at the heart of it all.
(Presenter LINK): reading article: Naidoo was hailed a hero. He “jumped from the moving vehicle” to shield his disoriented colleagues and continued fighting [on foot]. Though he was badly injured — bleeding from his head — he refused to leave the scene, staying until the SAPS dog unit arrived, and then helped track the fleeing suspects.
(Presenter VO): For his courage, he received a bravery award from the SAPS.
(Presenter VO): Munsami, was also seriously injured — his face was shattered in the crash and he required facial reconstructive surgery, including the insertion of a metal plate.
(LINK): Munsamy was left with poor eyesight and Naidoo has since been plagued by persistent migraine headaches. We don't have full medical records, but these injuries raise an important question: How fit were these officers for active duty at the time of the Ismail shooting?
Expert Commentary: A lot of the time there’s pressure from within SAPS for officers to remain on active duty, even when carrying significant injuries. Sometimes it’s the officers themselves who want to continue, especially if they see themselves as still capable or feel a sense of duty.
VO: We reached out to the officers involved for their responses.
ON SCREEN: Officers’ Response: They said they couldn’t speak because of their upcoming cases.
SAPS Response: [Insert official SAPS comment or refusal to comment.]
NPA Response: [Insert National Prosecuting Authority’s official stance on the case and the delays.]
IPID Response: [Insert Independent Police Investigative Directorate’s comment on the stalled investigation and scene-handling concerns.]

(Presenter VO/LINK): Was there ever an Etios? Who fired first? Why was no ambulance called? These are questions that can only be answered in court. But are they questions these officers want the public to know? I guess we’ll wait and see, but for now the Ismail family are waiting for justice. There is some good news.
Incredibly, baby Essa survived — he turns five this month.









Summary:
TREATMENT:
Story Arc:
Opening Sequence – 1:30
We open with two parallel narratives:
• The Ismail family: Omar, Asma, and toddler Yusraa heading home after visiting Asma’s mother.
• The police: National Intervention Unit officers preparing to intercept hijackers in a silver Toyota Etios.
Both stories collide in the shootout. We frame the piece as a mystery — not revealing immediately that the shooters are police, nor casting doubt on the Etios’s existence yet. Instead, we simply say that everyone’s lives change in an instant.
We hint at the bigger theme: justice delayed, perhaps denied — and that our search for answers leads to revelations more disturbing than the shooting itself.
ACT 1: ACT 1 – The Ismail Family’s Story
We go into Omar and Asma’s account in detail, building tension toward two major twists:
1. After the shooting, Asma’s mother discovers the gunmen are police.
2. The police haven’t called emergency services.
We do scene setting: Give a sense of where this happened a map introduce the re-enactments and graphic representations of the shootout.
We also show how the accident has affected the family to continue the storytelling.
ACT 2: ACT 2 – The Police Officers’ Story
We introduce the officers and their version, reconstructed from documents and affidavits. Their right of reply (their legal defences and reasoning) is woven in here, not tacked on at the end. This will allow the journalism to show without ruining the story.
The tension here lies with the blame the police lay on Omar, citing volenti non fit injuria — essentially claiming he knowingly drove into a gunfight. At this point, we haven’t yet revealed that there’s no evidence of an Etios, so the audience is still piecing it together.
We then start dismantling the police’s account:
• Was there an Etios?
• What did witnesses see?
• What do the ballistics and scene reports say?
We link this to Asma’s shocking account of how Omar was shot, leading to the question: if the family had died, would this version have gone unchallenged?
ACT 3 – Law, Delays, and a Twist
We break down what the law says about use of force — officers can only fire in self-defence or in defence of others. If there were no hijackers, this defence collapses.
We look at the stalled investigations — by the Hawks, IPID, and the NPA — despite compelling evidence. Then comes the final twist: could the delays be due to inefficiency and bureaucracy… or the fact that some of these officers are celebrated heroes?
We reveal their role in the high-profile N2 shootout, using passionate media coverage from the time.
Finally, we seek direct responses:
• From each officer.
• From SAPS, NPA, and IPID.
We close with a small moment of hope: Baby Essa, in Asma’s womb that night, survived. He turns five next week.

Further information:
VISUALS PLAN
We have a rare opportunity: 6–10 key documents that can be shown on screen. This allows us to:
1. Present the police officers’ own version of events (covering us for right of reply).
2. Juxtapose their account against the Ismail family’s version — then highlight contradictions.
Document & Narrative Integration
• Use a mix of dramatizations, recreations, and graphic representations to illustrate both sides.
• TIMELAPSES…
• Consider AI-generated stills or composites for moments we can’t physically film.
• For the police version, tread carefully: we have their photos — but need to decide if we can legally name or show them.
• Question for legal: Can we name them on-screen? Can we show photographs?
Vehicles
• We can hire a white VW Polo for reenactments.
• Consider sourcing a white BMW (similar to the police’s) for accuracy in police-perspective shots.
Night & Day Coverage
• Recreate parts of the incident at night for authenticity and at day for clarity.
• Question: Do we film at the actual scene? If yes, security arrangements are essential — Berea at night can be risky.
________________________________________
FAMILY INTERVIEWS
• Omar & Asma: Film at their home.
o Option 1: Interview with personal items/photos visible in background (similar to the Harri story).
o Option 2: Neutral setup with framed wall of photos.
• Asma:
o In burqa — film her walking to subtly show her lost leg (using x-rays as supporting visuals).
o Capture her doing everyday tasks at home.
o Likely no filming inside the Ampath lab, so recreate work at home.
• Omar:
o Possibly film in the Polo as part of reenactment (without taking them to the actual scene, which they avoid).
• Rehana (mother):
o Interview at the scene in daylight — walk-and-talk explaining positions and events.
________________________________________
EXPERT INTERVIEWS
• Decide on setting: studio-style, in-the-field, or scene-adjacent.
• Consider visuals that make expert commentary dynamic (e.g., standing near scene diagrams, interactive graphics).
________________________________________
RIGHT OF REPLY
• We have contact numbers for all the officers.
• Plan: Call them from a quiet location (possibly inside a vehicle for controlled sound) and request on-camera comment.
• Expect they will refer us to legal counsel or cite sub judice.
• Portrayal decision: How do we integrate their refusal or limited response into the story?
• Timeline: Send questions only after family interviews (to avoid jeopardising them).

MacFarlane went on a journey of twists and surprises — and it all comes down to who you believe. INTRO (Presenter VO): As the Ismail family drove home in July 2020, they never imagined that, seconds later, as they passed this cemetery, they would be knocking on death’s door. (Presenter VO): In the years that followed, questions remain unanswered. (Omar): Why would someone want to shoot us? (Naidoo subtitle): Why would we come now and shoot this Polo? What is so special about this car? (Presenter VO): Two versions of that night emerged — one from the shooters, one from the family in the line of fire. Who is telling the truth? A complex question… when the shooters were the police. (Presenter LINK 1): This story is about what happens when those we trust to protect us cause irreparable harm instead. It’s also about justice denied, and perhaps delayed. Five years on and the shooting that tore the Ismail family’s lives apart, and no one has been held accountable. ACT 1: The Ismail Family Version (Presenter VO): It’s a cold winter evening in Berea, Durban… Omar Ismail drives home with his wife, Asma, and their toddler, Yusraa. Asma sits in the back beside Yusraa, snug in her car seat. As the family approaches hill street, a white BMW suddenly cuts them off. (Omar): Two guys jumped out from the front left hand side, jumped out and both of them started opening fire. These people are trying to kill us. I’m not sure if those people are hijackers or what. But there was no warning shots. (Asma): It was just a whole lot of shattering glass and metal. You know honestly there was no time to react, I took cover and I was clutching my daughter. I hadn't heard gunshots before, so to make sense of what was happening, You know, realizing that this is a shooting. (Presenter VO): Omar ducks behind the steering wheel — their silver Polo hits the BMW. (Omar): And that's when I picked my head up and that's when I got shot in the back of my head. (Asma): That for me was the most horrific moment, seeing him getting shot, it was very purposeful. We were stationary at that point and whoever had shot him, they knew exactly what they were doing. (Mac): They were trying to kill him? (Asma): They were trying to kill him. There was just blood shooting out at the back of his head. I realised that I was injured, my foot is lying under the seat in front of me. Mac: Ooh okay. (Asma): And that it's not attached to me anymore. (Presenter VO): Little Yusraa - shot in her arm - is saved by her car seat. Omar is shot three times, and left temporarily blind. Amid the chaos, they have no idea that their assailants are policemen. (Omar): I was really shocked. It was like your heart just drops completely knowing that police, the guys who were meant to protect you, are the ones that shot us. (Presenter link): But what really happened at this T-junction? The story the police would later tell would make the family question everything. (Presenter VO): On that July evening… Six highly trained officers from the National Intervention Unit are hunting hijackers. They’re dressed in tactical gear but driving unmarked cars: a white BMW and a Kombi. In their affidavits, the officers will say they have intel that the hijackers are in a silver Toyota Etios. Three of the officers fire shots: Donovan Naidoo, Meziwa Shabalala, and Yogandran Munsami. (Presenter link): Carte Blanche has sifted through witness statements, ballistics tests, expert analyses, and hours of CCTV footage — and we’ve uncovered evidence that pokes glaring holes in the police’s account. (Presenter VO): Critical to the police version is the silver Etios. But was there an Etios on the scene at all? There’s no footage of the shooting, but CCTV shows the family’s Polo 300m before the scene… What’s missing? There’s no silver Etios behind it. (Naidoo): The Etios was recovered. (Das Neves): But even if there was a second vehicle, it has no bearing on who the police were firing at on the day. The fact of the matter is, those rounds struck where the guns were aimed at. (Presenter VO): Lobo Das Neves is a law enforcement expert. (Das Neves): No arrest of any suspect supersedes the safety and security of a member of the public. (Presenter VO): As for the Etios recovered two weeks later — sources close to the investigation say they found no link between it and the shooting. And the family is concerned it was found by the same officers involved in the shooting. (Das Neves): The moment an investigator becomes involved in an active shooting, that investigator now becomes a witness. Or, in some cases, a suspect, and which makes whatever evidence they collected very, very questionable. (Presenter VO): On closer inspection, we find the roof of the recovered Etios isn’t the same as the one in the CCTV footage. This means they’re different vehicles! (Presenter VO): What about ballistic evidence? Two ballistics reports agree that none of the bullets damaged the car’s passenger side - the side police say hijackers fired from. (Naidoo): There is not a single bullet where ballistics can confirm that these bullets are from the SAPS. (Presenter VO): This is because the bullets are too damaged from impact to be matched to weapons. Meanwhile, witnesses allege that they saw officers collecting spent cartridges after the shooting. (Das Neves): The only shell casings that were collected were those that were fired by the police and not by the perpetrators, which is enough evidence to reasonably suspect that it was a one-way firing exercise and not a two-way firing exercise. CUT TO: NIU police officers gearing up — hands loading magazines, a rifle’s bolt clacking into place. Police radio: “We’re looking for a silver Etios.” The screech of brakes. A deafening volley of gunshots. Screams pierce the chaos. Photos from scene after shooting… emergency lights and noises… (Presenter VO):— The years that followed that moment have been riddled with questions… SOUNDUPS: QUESTIONS Two versions of that night emerged — one from the shooters, one from the family in the line of fire. Who is telling the truth? (Presenter LINK): This is about what happens when those we trust to protect us may have instead caused irreparable harm. But it’s more than that — it’s about justice delayed, and perhaps denied. Five years on from the shooting that tore the Ismail family’s lives apart, no one has been held to account. And the reasons may be as disturbing as the shooting itself. FADE TO BLACK… ACT 1: The basic story (Presenter VO): A cold winter Thursday evening — around 7 p.m., July 16, 2020 — settles over Berea, Durban. Omar Ismail drives home with his wife, Asma, and their toddler, Yusraa, after visiting Asma’s mother. Ten weeks pregnant with their second child — a little boy they plan to name Essa — Asma sits in the back seat beside Yusraa, strapped into her car seat. (Asma): (Omar): (Presenter VO): A few hundred metres from their home on Sheringham Road, a white unmarked BMW suddenly swerves into the road. A man jumps out, gun in hand. (Asma): (Omar): (Presenter VO): Omar ducks beneath the steering wheel to avoid the bullets, unable to see clearly — their silver Polo hits the BMW and they drift into a streetlamp. (Asma): (Omar): (Presenter VO): Then… silence. Yusraa is screaming. While trying to make sense of what just happened. Omar lifts his head — another shot rings out from behind. The bullet tears through the headrest, hitting him in the back of the head. He slumps forward. Asma, her right leg hanging by a thread clings to consciousness. She calls her mother, Rehana. Visual: Mother answering the phone, horrified. Rehana: It was close to their house — maybe five minutes away. I drove straight there. (Presenter VO): What she finds is an unexpected twist. Rehana: “When I arrived, the men told me they were police officers. (Presenter VO): But that's not the only strange information she learns. Rehana: But there was something wrong — no ambulance, no flashing lights. They hadn’t called emergency services. It had been nearly ten minutes, and I was the first to phone for an ambulance.” Visual: Photos of vehicles and bullet damage at the scene. (Presenter VO): Asma’s heart stops at St Augustine’s Hospital, but she’s resuscitated. Yusraa - shot in her arm - was luckily saved by her car seat. Omar was shot four times, including his head, and was left temporarily blind. Visual: Timelapse sky, fading to black. (Presenter LINK) with family: “Months later, Omar was left with shrapnel in his brain, and risks paralysis if surgeons attempt removal. Asma lost her right leg and she still has shrapnel in her left. (Presenter VO): Asma works as a lab technician, and standing for hours is painful. Omar, a bookkeeper, has struggled to find employment since the shooting, his current job is made more difficult by his partial blindness and severe headaches. (Presenter LINK) at Intersection: But what really happened at this T-junction of Hill and Sheringham Roads? The story the police would later tell would make the family question everything. This is their story according to their pleas and affidavits. Fade to black… ACT 2: The Two Versions Military-style, authoritative tone; overlay of visuals and VO ON SCREEN: 16 July 2020… Presenter VO (dramatic tone): “Six police officers are on the hunt for a group of hijackers. On-Screen Visuals: Fade into uniformed officers preparing for deployment. (Presenter VO): They’re members of the National Intervention Unit (NIU)—an elite, intelligence-driven tactical unit in the South African Police Service trained for high-risk operations such as armed crime, and violent syndicate activity. They report directly to the National Commissioner of Police. (Presenter VO): Crime Intelligence’s information is that the syndicate’s suspects are in the Berea area—travelling in a silver or grey Toyota Etios sedan with cloned plates. Visual overlay: Show a schematic of two unmarked vehicles in convoy. (Presenter LINK): The Warrant officers wore uniforms but their two vehicles were unmarked. In the BMW (white 1 series) was Talent Mseleku the driver, Yogandran Munsami and Donovan Naidoo. Following them in a VW Kombi (silver) was driver Menzi Michael Shabalala and Mathew Nathoo. ON SCREEN graphic: Display 18:45 over a map. (Presenter VO): As the convoy drove South along Hill Street toward Sheringham Road, the officers in the BMW noticed a silver VW Polo - that’s the Ismail family - but ALSO the silver Toyota Etios they’ve been looking for behind it. It’s implied the Polo and Etios were stationary when the police came across them. They say —”the hijackers alighted their vehicle and were about to hijack the VW Polo when NIU members intervened.” [page 2, iii]. Presenter LINK (raising questions): “The police’s descriptions of the hijackers is scant. They’re male, although the number remains unknown. All that’s reported is that they were wearing balaclavas and were moving in a crouched-over manner toward the VW Polo’s rear. [no where does it say they were stationary] (Presenter VO): Munsami leapt from the front passenger seat of the BMW, shouting ‘POLICE!’ They say the hijackers then opened fire — and that’s when the gunfight began. The police say their shots were aimed at the hijackers in the Toyota Etios, and that the Ismail family’s Polo was caught in the crossfire. They say it wasn’t their bullets that struck Omar, Asma, and Yusraa — but the hijackers. And even if their own rounds did cause the injuries, their defense is that it was a lawful shooting, undertaken to protect the family from a ‘dangerous situation.’ (Presenter LINK): The officers frame their actions as those of ‘peace officers’ defending themselves and the public. Their legal defence even leans on an obscure doctrine — volenti non fit injuria — which means Omar knowingly drove into the line of fire. (Presenter VO): The hijackers fled down Sheringham Road. Shabalala, in the VW Kombi, returned fire while Naidoo shot the Etios’s rear tyre. Mseleku attempted to give chase, but due to the collision with the Polo the BMW was too damaged. After they say they checked on the Polo’s occupants and called for medical assistance. Presenter LINK to next section: Who’s really telling the truth? Carte Blanche has sifted through witness statements, ballistics tests, expert analyses, and hours of CCTV footage — uncovering evidence that punches glaring holes in the police’s account. And it starts with the shocking revelation: Was there a silver Etios? TEXT ON SCREEN: Was there an Etios? (Omar): No car was following us. (Presenter VO):There are nine CCTV camera angles covering different points along this route. They reveal the police’s timeline is out by 15 minutes, but when you track the Ismail family’s Polo across multiple points… even a few hundred metres before the shooting…the evidence is in what you don’t see. No Etios... In fact, there’s no footage of an Etios in any footage. EXPERT INTRO (EXPERT): CCTV footage doesn’t lie — timestamps are locked, and the sequence can be independently verified. This raises serious questions about the police version. (Presenter VO): But it does show something the police left out — the VW Kombi missed the turn into Hill Street, and therefore, was about a minute behind the BMW. That likely means they weren’t there when the first shots were fired — at least not as the police’s version infers. VISUAL: TEXT ON SCREEN: What did witnesses see? (Presenter VO): There were many witnesses like blah blah who we met at the scene. It's what two witnesses for the Ismail family saw, or didn't see, is critical. He also says the police were firing directly at the Polo. Could this have been a case of mistaken identity? (Expert): This points to a likely case of mistaken identity. From the front, a silver VW Polo and a silver Toyota Etios can look similar — but if there was no Etios at all, it suggests the police account of suspects and their behaviour was fabricated. Presenter LINK: Witness Two only heard the gunfire. When he dared to look outside, he also saw no Etios. But he noticed something else — something darker. The officers were collecting their spent cartridges. Was there a coverup? (Expert): That’s scene tampering. Removing shell casings prevents ballistic experts from matching a bullet to a specific gun — and to the officer who fired it. TEXT ON SCREEN: What do the bullets and scene say? Another graphic - we also have photos from SAPS scene recreation report. (Presenter VO): “There are two ballistic reports: the state’s and the family’s. Both agree there were no shell casings, but the eight R4/R5 rifle rounds they did find, were likely from police weapons. But the family’s expert found something more — a ninth bullet from a 9mm pistol. Remember that extra bullet for later. LINK: Both experts also agree on this: there was no crossfire. All the shots came from the direction of the police. The family’s expert says the Polo was deliberately targeted; the state’s expert stops short of saying that outright — but the implication is clear. (Presenter VO): A SAPS scene reconstruction aligns with the Ismail family’s version confirming the Polo was moving and not stationary as the police’s version implies. And that the direction of fire was at the Polo, this resulted in Omar likely panicking and losing control of the vehicle. (Expert): That’s a critical point — it places the Ismail family directly in the line of police fire from the outset. It was because they shot at him that he ducked. LINK: If this was a case of mistaken identity, when did the officers realise they had the wrong car — at the moment Omar’s Polo slammed into their BMW, or when they heard the baby screaming? The missing shell casings and a specific moment during the shooting cast a dark shadow over the officers’ actions. Asma: That must have been when the officers realised something was wrong — what hijacker would have a baby in the car? My husband then popped up his head. VO: Omar had been crouched low behind the steering wheel, then raised his head. Omar: I just wanted to check on them. Presenter: Can you remember that? Omar: Yes. Asma: I was already calling my mother, panicking, trying to get help. And then I saw one of the men with a gun coming closer to the window — and he fired into the driver’s headrest. Omar slumped forward. Rehana (Asma’s mother): I thought my son-in-law was dead. VO: Could this have been from the missing 9mm round? Rehana kept having this question running through her mind. Rehana: Why hadn’t the police called an ambulance? Link: Was there a coverup? Missing shell casings, no ambulances called, the extra bullet round, when and how Omar was shot… It begs the logical question: If the Ismail family didn’t survive, would these events have died with them? ACT 3: TEXT ON SCREEN: What does the Law say? (Expert): It’s also important to consider who fired first. If there were no hijackers, the first shots could only have come from the police. That’s a serious problem — it opens the door to attempted murder charges. Our law is clear: force can only be used in self-defence or to protect others. That clearly doesn’t apply here. Presenter LINK: And yet, years later, the case has stalled. Omar: The NPA says it is still waiting for the Hawks to act. IPID — the Independent Police Investigative Directorate — has also investigated, but that too has gone nowhere. (Expert): When IPID arrives on a scene, their job is to secure the shooting site, investigate whether evidence — like shell casings — was tampered with, and confiscate the firearms used. If those steps weren’t followed immediately, it undermines the entire investigation. Presenter VO: But what about the civil case? That case names the Police Ministry itself, that seeks to awards money to the family for the damage this has caused. Omar: It was supposed to go ahead in September last year, then again this September. But they keep delaying it — getting new lawyers. Instead of settling with us, it’s costing the state hundreds of thousands. I don’t know if they’re hoping we’ll die or something before that from our injuries. (Expert): In law, there’s a provision against wasteful and fruitless expenditure. The police should recognise they have no realistic chance of winning and settle with the family. Continuing to fight is already costing taxpayers hundreds of thousands. (Presenter VO): We asked the police how much they’ve spent defending the civil case. [N2](Presenter LINK): And we wanted to know why there have been such long delays in investigating these officers. Is it simply inefficiency, indifference, or bureaucracy? Or… could it be because two of the officers involved in the shooting are celebrated police heroes? That’s why I’m standing here — on this stretch of Durban’s N2 highway near Nandi Drive. TEXT ON SCREEN: August 4, 2017. TEXT ON SCREEN: August 4, 2017 (Presenter VO): In August 2017, two of the officers now implicated in the Ismail family shooting — Donovan Naidoo and Yogandran Munsamy — were involved in a high-profile shootout. In that daylight battle, five armed suspects were intercepted; three “died at the scene,” while two survived and were arrested. Civilians and officers were injured in the chaos. Naidoo and Munsamy were at the heart of it all. (Presenter LINK): reading article: Naidoo was hailed a hero. He “jumped from the moving vehicle” to shield his disoriented colleagues and continued fighting [on foot]. Though he was badly injured — bleeding from his head — he refused to leave the scene, staying until the SAPS dog unit arrived, and then helped track the fleeing suspects. (Presenter VO): For his courage, he received a bravery award from the SAPS. (Presenter VO): Munsami, was also seriously injured — his face was shattered in the crash and he required facial reconstructive surgery, including the insertion of a metal plate. (LINK): Munsamy was left with poor eyesight and Naidoo has since been plagued by persistent migraine headaches. We don't have full medical records, but these injuries raise an important question: How fit were these officers for active duty at the time of the Ismail shooting? Expert Commentary: A lot of the time there’s pressure from within SAPS for officers to remain on active duty, even when carrying significant injuries. Sometimes it’s the officers themselves who want to continue, especially if they see themselves as still capable or feel a sense of duty. SAPS Response: [Insert official SAPS comment or refusal to comment.] NPA Response: [Insert National Prosecuting Authority’s official stance on the case and the delays.] IPID Response: [Insert Independent Police Investigative Directorate’s comment on the stalled investigation and scene-handling concerns.] (Presenter VO/LINK): Was there ever an Etios? Who fired first? Why was no ambulance called? These are questions that can only be answered in court. But are they questions these officers want the public to know? I guess we’ll wait and see, but for now the Ismail family are waiting for justice. There is some good news. Incredibly, baby Essa survived — he turns five this month.
metadata.Summary: TREATMENT: Story Arc: Opening Sequence – 1:30 We open with two parallel narratives: • The Ismail family: Omar, Asma, and toddler Yusraa heading home after visiting Asma’s mother. • The police: National Intervention Unit officers preparing to intercept hijackers in a silver Toyota Etios. Both stories collide in the shootout. We frame the piece as a mystery — not revealing immediately that the shooters are police, nor casting doubt on the Etios’s existence yet. Instead, we simply say that everyone’s lives change in an instant. We hint at the bigger theme: justice delayed, perhaps denied — and that our search for answers leads to revelations more disturbing than the shooting itself. ACT 1: ACT 1 – The Ismail Family’s Story We go into Omar and Asma’s account in detail, building tension toward two major twists: 1. After the shooting, Asma’s mother discovers the gunmen are police. 2. The police haven’t called emergency services. We do scene setting: Give a sense of where this happened a map introduce the re-enactments and graphic representations of the shootout. We also show how the accident has affected the family to continue the storytelling. ACT 2: ACT 2 – The Police Officers’ Story We introduce the officers and their version, reconstructed from documents and affidavits. Their right of reply (their legal defences and reasoning) is woven in here, not tacked on at the end. This will allow the journalism to show without ruining the story. The tension here lies with the blame the police lay on Omar, citing volenti non fit injuria — essentially claiming he knowingly drove into a gunfight. At this point, we haven’t yet revealed that there’s no evidence of an Etios, so the audience is still piecing it together. We then start dismantling the police’s account: • Was there an Etios? • What did witnesses see? • What do the ballistics and scene reports say? We link this to Asma’s shocking account of how Omar was shot, leading to the question: if the family had died, would this version have gone unchallenged? ACT 3 – Law, Delays, and a Twist We break down what the law says about use of force — officers can only fire in self-defence or in defence of others. If there were no hijackers, this defence collapses. We look at the stalled investigations — by the Hawks, IPID, and the NPA — despite compelling evidence. Then comes the final twist: could the delays be due to inefficiency and bureaucracy… or the fact that some of these officers are celebrated heroes? We reveal their role in the high-profile N2 shootout, using passionate media coverage from the time. Finally, we seek direct responses: • From each officer. • From SAPS, NPA, and IPID. We close with a small moment of hope: Baby Essa, in Asma’s womb that night, survived. He turns five next week.
